Forced feeding began shortly before midnight on January 26, after roughly 106 hours without food, and was repeated about twelve times by February 1. Governor Charles S. Whitman pardoned her at about 7 p.m. on February 1, 1917, conditional on her not repeating the offence, and she was removed from the island at about 10:30 that night. The sentence ended by pardon — not by completion and not by reversal of the conviction. records.name: John Soderberg

records.name: John Swanson

records.name: John T. Gojack

United States, 384 U.S. 702, 705. The Supreme Court reversed that conviction on June 13, 1966. The reviewed court records do not establish individual physical custody dates; neither sentence is counted as time actually served.
records.after: Nine months, stayed pending appeal and conviction reversed; three months and a $200 fine on retrial, also reversed.

records.after: Concurrent terms of up to eighteen months; conviction reversed.

records.name: Julián Montalan
records.before:
Captured during the suppression of the Sakay movement and reportedly given a life sentence; exact arrest and release dates are less complete than for Sakay and Carreón, so release date is omitted.

The Philippine Bureau of Prisons catalogue, revised June 1927, confirms that Montalan was serving a life term at Iwahig in 1914. It reports that he subsequently received executive clemency, conditional on not returning to the provinces associated with his case. The report does not give the date of clemency or physical release.
records.after: Life; conditional clemency prohibiting return to designated provinces.

records.after: Ninety days, eighty suspended; ten unsuspended days reducible to five for good behavior.

records.name: Junius Scales
records.before: Six years in federal prison. He was free pending litigation and appeals for nearly seven years after his arrest, and was ordered to surrender to the United States marshal in New York City at noon on October 2, 1961, after the Supreme Court affirmed the conviction. He served 448 days — fourteen months and twenty-two days, conventionally reported as fifteen months — at the United States Penitentiary at Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, until President John F. Kennedy commuted the remainder of the sentence on December 24, 1962 and he left Lewisburg that same Christmas Eve. The action was a commutation, not a pardon: the conviction remained legally intact. He was the last Smith Act prisoner released.
